title: Phase 14: Design Documents and Conformance Policy
description:
Build a policy scanner that continuously evaluates whether the system’s design documentation is complete, current, internally consistent, and aligned with the implemented codebase.

The scanner must maintain an up-to-date inventory of Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), Product Requirements Documents (PRDs), engineering design documents, and other authoritative design artifacts. Each artifact should be linked to the code, components, interfaces, architectural regions, requirements, and decisions that it governs.

For every review target, the scanner should compare:

Declared intent — the requirements, constraints, decisions, and expected behavior documented in PRDs, ADRs, and engineering designs.
Observed implementation — the structure and behavior evident in the current code, tests, configuration, schemas, and public interfaces.
Change history — how both the implementation and governing documentation have evolved.
Current conformance — whether the implementation satisfies the documented intent and architectural constraints.

Where differences are found, the scanner must determine whether they indicate:

An incomplete implementation.
Incorrect behavior or a likely defect.
A missing or violated architectural constraint.
An undocumented design decision.
Architectural drift.
An implementation improvement that remains within the scope of the governing ADR or design.
A valid evolution that requires the ADR, PRD, or design document to be updated or superseded.
An ambiguous condition requiring human review.

The scanner must not assume that either the documentation or the implementation is automatically correct. Findings should identify the conflict, cite evidence from both sources, explain the likely impact, and recommend an appropriate resolution. Recommendations may include correcting the code, adding tests, updating documentation, clarifying requirements, amending an ADR, or creating a new superseding ADR.

The scanner is advisory and reporting-only. It must not modify source code or design documentation automatically.

Functional requirements
Discover and index all ADRs, PRDs, and engineering design documents.
Detect missing, duplicate, obsolete, orphaned, or conflicting design artifacts.
Validate ADR metadata, status, relationships, and supersession chains.
Link design artifacts to:
Crates, packages, modules, services, and components.
APIs, schemas, data models, and configuration.
Architectural regions and subsystem boundaries.
Requirements, tests, and implementation targets.
Other governing or dependent design documents.
Support explicit links declared in metadata and inferred links discovered through analysis.
Distinguish authoritative relationships from inferred relationships.
Assess the confidence of inferred links and findings.
Detect code that lacks an identifiable governing requirement or design decision.
Detect design requirements with no corresponding implementation or verification.
Compare implementation behavior with documented requirements and constraints.
Evaluate whether code changes remain within the scope of existing ADRs.
Identify architectural drift across revisions rather than examining only the current snapshot.
Detect contradictions between ADRs, PRDs, engineering designs, tests, and implementation.
Produce actionable, evidence-based findings without changing the repository.
Finding format

Each finding should contain:

Unique finding identifier.
Title and category.
Severity and confidence.
Governing design artifacts.
Affected code and architectural region.
Declared intent.
Observed implementation.
Description of the discrepancy.
Evidence with precise file and symbol locations.
Expected or potential impact.
Historical context, when relevant.
Recommended resolution.
Suggested disposition:
Fix implementation.
Complete implementation.
Add or correct tests.
Update design documentation.
Amend existing ADR.
Create a superseding ADR.
Clarify ownership or scope.
Accept and record intentional drift.
Require human review.
Acceptance criteria
All supported design documents appear in a searchable design-artifact index.
Each architectural region identifies its governing ADRs, requirements, and engineering designs where known.
Each relationship records whether it is explicit or inferred, including confidence and supporting evidence.
The scanner reports unimplemented requirements, undocumented implementation, contradictory decisions, stale documents, and architectural drift.
Findings cite precise document sections and code locations.
The scanner distinguishes code defects from valid architectural evolution.
Existing ADRs are never silently rewritten to match current implementation.
A recommendation to update an ADR explains why the implementation represents a valid evolution rather than an accidental divergence.
Findings can be suppressed or accepted only with a recorded rationale, owner, and optional expiration or review date.
Repeated scans produce stable identifiers so findings can be tracked over time.
The scanner remains reporting-only and makes no automatic repository changes.
